lines: Here, {gift_item}. The right tool in the right hand saves a lot of trouble.
Take {gift_item}. Keep it useful and it will repay you twice.
Good. {gift_item} did the job for {tested_villager}.
Then the advice had a good edge. {tested_villager} liked {gift_item}.
Wrong tool for the work. For {gift_subject}, use {alternative_gift} instead.
{gift_item} slipped in the hand? Try {alternative_gift}; cleaner work.

messages.text: Wrong tool, wrong job. Pick up {alternative_gift} next time.
You used the advice as-is? Hm. Sharpen your judgment and bring {alternative_gift}.

openings.text: Mind the smithing table. What do you need?

closings.text: Back to making tools that do not fail, then.

pacify.text: Fine. I will put the edge away, for now.
Wrong measure. It takes {emerald_cost} {emeralds} to set this right.
No. You are using {payment_items} like the wrong tool.

lines: Cracked handles are small warnings with expensive timing.
A dull edge makes every simple job into a bad plan.
A handle should fit the hand, not argue with it.
A sharp edge is useful. A careless one is just trouble with shine.
The bench hears every complaint before the finished tool gets praised.
Cracked handles are warnings. Ignore them and they become stories.
A good tool is quiet proof that someone cared before trouble started.
I once fixed a pick that had seen more stone than sense.
A shovel broke on me once because I asked it to do axe work.

lines.text: Mind the table. Good tools begin with nobody bumping my elbow.
Tool jokes work better when they have a point. Mine sometimes have two.
That idea is bent past repair.
You are using your manners like the wrong tool for the job.

lines: I remember my mind working again, like a tool freed from rust.
You put a handle back on my life when I could not grip it myself.
Your face fits the memory, though the memory is still badly forged.
I remember a cure biting harder than a dull saw, then sense returning.

lines.text: I remember you. The old fear still catches like a nicked blade.

lines: Thunder shook the smithing table so hard loose tools danced on the bench, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked tools, handles, and repair scraps after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the smithing table, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the tool handles twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have tool handles to set right.
I checked wooden handles and coal dust for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the smithing table after.
The tools can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the smithing table, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the smithing table, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, the tools can wait on the bench; who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the smithing table still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before tools, handles, and repair scraps. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the smithing table and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the smithing table, I saw fear cross the square; then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the smithing table first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the tool rack by the door and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the smithing table enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a mended handle between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the smithing table, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning grit from the hinges.
I checked tools, handles, and repair scraps, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the smithing table, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a toolsmith which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the smithing table, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
The tools can wait on the bench. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the smithing table found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the smithing table. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing ice off the shovel blades and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the smithing table. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
